lead: Phase equilibrium is the state where every component has the same fugacity in every phase present. For one pure substance that equality fixes the vapour pressure at each temperature. For a mixture it fixes two curves: the bubble line and the dew line. Those curves are the working maps for distillation, flash drums, condensers and LPG storage. This chapter reads the maps from fugacity equality, without adding activity coefficients yet.
prereq: You need the fugacity and chemical-potential criterion from 6.1, fugacity definitions from Unit 5, and the Clausius-Clapeyron equation from Unit 4.

sections.h3: Pure component: one curve from fugacity equality

blocks.text: At saturation a pure liquid and its vapour coexist. Equilibrium requires equal temperature, equal pressure and equal fugacity. For a fixed T only one pressure satisfies f<sup>L</sup>=f<sup>V</sup>. That pressure is P<sup>sat</sup>(T), the vapour pressure. Its plot against T is the vapour-pressure curve. On a P-T diagram it ends at the triple point and the critical point; fusion and sublimation curves meet it at the triple point.

blocks.where: f<sup>L</sup> and f<sup>V</sup> are the liquid and vapour fugacities in the same pressure unit; P<sup>sat</sup> is the saturation vapour pressure; T is absolute temperature.

blocks.text: The Antoine equation fits the curve over a modest range. The constants A, B and C belong to one unit set. A set with P in mmHg and T in °C is not interchangeable with one using kPa and K. Check the units before substituting.

blocks.where: P<sup>sat</sup> is vapour pressure in the unit of the table; T is temperature in the unit of the table; A, B and C are fitted constants.

blocks.text: The slope gives latent heat. From Unit 4, two vapour pressures at T<sub>1</sub> and T<sub>2</sub> give Δh<sub>vap</sub> = R ln(P<sub>2</sub>/P<sub>1</sub>)/(1/T<sub>1</sub> − 1/T<sub>2</sub>).

blocks.where: Δh<sub>vap</sub> is enthalpy of vaporization in J/mol; R = 8.314 J mol<sup>−1</sup> K<sup>−1</sup>; T is absolute temperature in K.

blocks.text: Pressure changes liquid fugacity at fixed T through the Poynting correction. It is small unless P is far from P<sup>sat</sup>.

blocks.where: V<sup>L</sup> is liquid molar volume in m³/mol; P is pressure; P<sup>sat</sup> is saturation pressure; R is the gas constant; T is absolute temperature.

blocks.text: For a mixture the equality is per component: f<sub>i</sub><sup>V</sup>=f<sub>i</sub><sup>L</sup> for every component i. At fixed T, a liquid of composition x has a bubble pressure where the first vapour bubble forms. A vapour of composition y has a dew pressure where the first liquid drop forms. The P-x-y diagram draws both at fixed T; the T-x-y diagram draws both at fixed P.
For the ideal liquid mixture used here, fiV=yiP and fiL=xiPisat. Then yiP=xiPisat. A non-ideal liquid adds γi, treated in 6.4.

blocks.where: x<sub>i</sub> is liquid mole fraction; y<sub>i</sub> is vapour mole fraction; P is total pressure; P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup> is pure i vapour pressure.

blocks.text: For a binary with x<sub>2</sub>=1−x<sub>1</sub> and y<sub>2</sub>=1−y<sub>1</sub>, the bubble pressure is P<sub>bub</sub> = x<sub>1</sub>P<sub>1</sub><sup>sat</sup> + x<sub>2</sub>P<sub>2</sub><sup>sat</sup> and the dew pressure is 1/P<sub>dew</sub> = y<sub>1</sub>/P<sub>1</sub><sup>sat</sup> + y<sub>2</sub>/P<sub>2</sub><sup>sat</sup>. At x<sub>1</sub>=0 and x<sub>1</sub>=1 the two curves meet the pure vapour pressures.

blocks.where: P<sub>bub</sub> is bubble pressure; P<sub>dew</sub> is dew pressure; x<sub>1</sub> and y<sub>1</sub> are mole fractions of component 1; P<sub>1</sub><sup>sat</sup> and P<sub>2</sub><sup>sat</sup> are pure-component vapour pressures.

blocks.text: The figure uses benzene(1)–toluene(2) at 373.15 K: P<sub>1</sub><sup>sat</sup>=180.1 kPa and P<sub>2</sub><sup>sat</sup>=74.2 kPa. The bubble line is P=74.2+105.9x<sub>1</sub>; the dew line is P=1/(y<sub>1</sub>/180.1+(1−y<sub>1</sub>)/74.2).

sections.h3: Tie lines, lever rule and azeotropes

blocks.text: Between the curves a mixture splits into liquid x and vapour y at the same T and P. A horizontal tie line joins x and y. For overall composition z<sub>1</sub> between x<sub>1</sub> and y<sub>1</sub>, the lever rule gives n<sub>L</sub>/n<sub>V</sub>=(y<sub>1</sub>−z<sub>1</sub>)/(z<sub>1</sub>−x<sub>1</sub>). The liquid fraction is (y<sub>1</sub>−z<sub>1</sub>)/(y<sub>1</sub>−x<sub>1</sub>); the vapour fraction is (z<sub>1</sub>−x<sub>1</sub>)/(y<sub>1</sub>−x<sub>1</sub>).

On a T-x-y diagram at fixed P, heating a liquid reaches the bubble line where the first vapour appears. Further heating reaches the dew line where the last drop disappears. Between the lines both phases exist. The tie line again joins x and y.

At an azeotrope the two branches touch and x<sub>1</sub>=y<sub>1</sub>. Vapour and liquid have the same composition, so simple distillation cannot change composition. Common azeotropes can be minimum-boiling or maximum-boiling; changing pressure can move or break them. See 6.4 for the activity-coefficient cause.

figure.caption: Benzene–toluene P-x-y diagram at 373.15 K. The bubble line is straight, the dew line bends below it, and both meet the pure vapour pressures at x₁=0 and x₁=1.

examples.question: Benzene(1)–toluene(2) at 373.15 K has P₁<sup>sat</sup> = 180.1 kPa and P₂<sup>sat</sup> = 74.2 kPa. (a) For a liquid with x₁ = 0.30, find the bubble pressure and vapour composition y₁. (b) For a vapour with y₁ = 0.30, find the dew pressure and liquid composition x₁.
steps: Write the data: P₁<sup>sat</sup>=180.1 kPa, P₂<sup>sat</sup>=74.2 kPa, x₁=0.30, y₁=0.30.
Dew pressure: 1/P<sub>dew</sub> = y₁/P₁<sup>sat</sup> +(1−y₁)/P₂<sup>sat</sup> =0.30/180.1+0.70/74.2 =0.0016657+0.0094340=0.0110997 kPa<sup>−1</sup>, so P<sub>dew</sub>=90.09 kPa.
examples.answer: The bubble point is 105.97 kPa with y₁ = 0.5099, and the dew point is 90.09 kPa with x₁ = 0.1501.
examples.check:
P1=180.1
P2=74.2
x1=0.30
Pb=P2+(P1-P2)*x1
y1=x1*P1/Pb
y1_given=0.30
Pd=1/(y1_given/P1+(1-y1_given)/P2)
x1_dew=y1_given*Pd/P1
print(f"{Pb:.2f}")
print(f"{y1:.4f}")
print(f"{Pd:.2f}")
print(f"{x1_dew:.4f}")

traps: Swapping x and y on a P-x-y diagram. The bubble line is read with liquid x; the dew line is read with vapour y.
Using Antoine constants without checking the unit set. P may be mmHg, kPa or bar, and T may be °C or K; mixing sets gives a wrong P<sup>sat</sup>.
Calling the bubble point and dew point the same thing. Bubble point is the first vapour from liquid; dew point is the first liquid from vapour.
Using a pure-component P<sup>sat</sup> for a mixture without the composition term. For an ideal mixture the term x<sub>i</sub>P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup> is essential.
Treating an azeotrope as a pure component. At an azeotrope x=y, but the mixture still has two components and the branches touch only at that point.

quiz.q: Define bubble point and dew point for a binary mixture at fixed pressure.
quiz.a: Bubble point is the temperature at which the first bubble of vapour forms from a liquid. Dew point is the temperature at which the first drop of liquid forms from a vapour.

quiz.q: Why does a pure substance have a single vapour pressure at a given temperature?
quiz.a: Because f<sup>L</sup>=f<sup>V</sup> is one equation in one unknown, P, at fixed T. Only the pressure where the liquid and vapour fugacities are equal is a saturation pressure.

quiz.q: Benzene(1)–toluene(2) at 373.15 K has P₁<sup>sat</sup>=180.1 kPa and P₂<sup>sat</sup>=74.2 kPa. For x₁=0.50, find the bubble pressure and y₁.
On a P-x-y diagram at fixed T, why does the dew curve lie below the bubble line for an ideal binary mixture?
quiz.a: The bubble line is a mole-fraction average of P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup>. The dew line is a harmonic-type average, 1/P=Σy<sub>i</sub>/P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup>. Condensation of a vapour needs a lower pressure than bubble formation from a liquid of the same overall composition.

quiz.q: Two vapour pressures are 10 kPa at 300 K and 20 kPa at 320 K. Estimate Δh<sub>vap</sub> using Clausius-Clapeyron.
What does the Poynting correction account for, and when is it small?
quiz.a: It accounts for the change in liquid fugacity when pressure changes from P<sup>sat</sup> to P. It is small when V<sup>L</sup>(P−P<sup>sat</sup>)/(RT) is much less than 1, usually near low pressure.

quiz.q: At an azeotrope x₁=y₁. What happens to a simple distillation and to the lever rule?
quiz.a: The tie line has zero composition difference, so the lever rule gives no separation in composition. Distillation cannot enrich beyond the azeotrope; vapour and liquid leave with the same composition.

quiz.q: Name the three coexistence lines on a pure-component P-T diagram and the point where they meet.
quiz.a: Fusion, vaporization and sublimation curves. They meet at the triple point.

beyond: Not for the exam. Process simulators store Antoine or larger vapour-pressure fits and solve the same fugacity equalities for every stage of a column. Azeotropic and pressure-swing distillation use the fact that x=y at an azeotrope and that pressure shifts the azeotrope. Search terms: flash calculation, dew-point algorithm, Rachford-Rice, Poynting correction, pressure-swing distillation.
